title: Thermal stress with one-eighth symmetry
summary: Use three true mirror planes to remove rigid motion while preserving thermal expansion; combine heating and pressure and check the exact displacement, stress and reaction.

steps.title: One eighth of a symmetric solid
steps.explain: Use a cube centred at the origin as an independently checkable teaching problem. The full cube is 1 m on each side; model only its positive octant. This teaches the symmetry/thermal-expansion decision in Fusion’s rotor tutorial without pretending a cube is the vendor’s disk-brake geometry.

steps.title: Units for a small expansion
steps.explain: Display lengths in millimetres and stresses in MPa. The geometry still uses explicit metre values.

steps.title: The octant
steps.explain: The three minimum faces lie on the full cube’s mirror planes x = 0, y = 0 and z = 0. All three maximum faces are physical outside faces.

steps.title: Elastic expansion
steps.explain: Use illustrative isotropic constants E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3 and α = 10⁻⁵ /K. They are exact inputs for this teaching model, not certified brake-rotor material data.

steps.title: Assign it
steps.explain: One Material on the one-eighth Body.

steps.title: Mesh the eighth
steps.explain: A 2 × 2 × 2 quadratic mesh is sufficient for this constant-stress, affine-displacement patch. The automated check repeats it at more than one mesh size.

steps.title: Mirror normal to x
steps.explain: Symmetry removes only the displacement normal to the plane. The face can still slide in y and z as the cube expands; clamping it would invent thermal stress.

steps.title: Mirror normal to y
steps.explain: The second true mirror plane removes uy, not the entire displacement vector.

steps.title: Mirror normal to z
steps.explain: The third true mirror plane removes uz. Together these three conditions eliminate rigid motion while allowing the exact thermal expansion.

steps.title: A 100 K temperature rise
steps.explain: A uniform 100 °C temperature against a 0 °C stress-free reference gives ΔT = 100 K. No conduction solve is needed because the temperature is specified uniformly; use the chaining tutorial for a solved nonuniform field.

steps.title: Pressure on the real outer face
steps.explain: Apply 10 MPa pressure on xmax. In the full cube the reflected xmin outside face carries the same inward pressure. Mirror planes are cuts through the solid; do not apply this outside pressure to them.

steps.title: Combine the two loads
steps.explain: Linear static thermoelasticity combines uniform thermal expansion with uniaxial compression. All three mirror constraints belong to this Step.

steps.title: Solve, then read components
steps.explain: At the outside corner [0.5 m, 0.5 m, 0.5 m], expect ux = 0.475 mm and uy = uz = 0.5075 mm. The stress is σxx = −10 MPa, σyy = σzz = 0 and von Mises = 10 MPa. A displacement magnitude is not any one of those components.

steps.title: Fit and inspect
steps.explain: Fit the octant, inspect the three mirror faces, then press Next. The displayed deformation scale may be exaggerated; the numerical probe uses actual displacements.

steps.title: Symmetry is a physical statement
steps.explain: Only use an eighth when geometry, material axes, temperature and mechanical loads reflect across all three planes. A hotter sector, an asymmetric bolt or an off-axis load invalidates this reduction.
steps.theory:
For uniform heating and compression $p$ in x, isotropic thermoelasticity gives $\epsilon_x=\alpha\Delta T-p/E$ and $\epsilon_y=\epsilon_z=\alpha\Delta T+\nu p/E$. Therefore $u_i=\epsilon_i x_i$. With $\Delta T=100\,\mathrm K$, $p=10\,\mathrm{MPa}$ and the stated constants, the corner components are **0.475, 0.5075 and 0.5075 mm**. Thermal strain itself creates no stress when expansion is free. The only nonzero direct stress is $\sigma_{xx}=-p$, and $\sigma_\mathrm{VM}=p$. The modeled pressure resultant is $p(0.5)^2=2.5\,\mathrm{MN}$; compare the x support reaction against it, not the full cube’s face force.

For a free-heating comparison, remove only `compression` from the Step’s loads and solve again: every corner component becomes 0.5 mm and stress vanishes. For a deliberate wrong-model check, clamp a mirror face in all directions: the expansion is then restrained and the stress no longer has this closed form.

**Other solvers:** Abaqus XSYMM/YSYMM/ZSYMM and a temperature predefined field, Ansys frictionless/symmetry planes with a thermal body load, and Nastran normal-component SPCs with a temperature load express the same reduction. Fusion’s Thermal Stress workflow similarly preserves expansion on symmetry planes.

Problem inspiration: [Autodesk Fusion thermal-stress tutorial](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/ENU/Fusion-Simulate/files/GUID-88BCA6F7-A333-41C8-AA35-703F6F99DE13.htm). This guide uses its own cube, loads and exact solution; it does not reproduce or validate the vendor’s brake rotor, yielding assessment or CAD simplification.
